This page contains no mathematics. It is a continuous passage of German prose, apparently lecture or reading notes on ancient Greek history, about the early reign of Philip II of Macedon (r. 359–336 BC). It continues from the previous page, which introduced Philip's accession and his invention of the phalanx.

The content, in order:
(1) The phalanx was heavy infantry armed with pikes 20–24 feet long. It was drawn up very densely, so it could not easily be broken through.
(2) Philip first disposed of his two rivals. He removed Pausanias by bribing the king of Thrace, who had been supporting him.
(3) He defeated Argaeus. He then returned all Athenian prisoners of war without ransom and 'ceded' Amphipolis to Athens.
(4) He made war on the Illyrians and Paeonians and beat them in 358 BC with his phalanx. He extended his territory to Lake Lychnitis (Lake Ohrid) and had himself proclaimed king.
(5) He then planned to bring the Greek coastal colonies under his rule. The next page continues with Amphipolis (357), Potidaea, the gold mines of Mt. Pangaeus, Thessaly and Olynthus.

There are no derivations, formulas, numbers of mathematical interest or computations to reconstruct.

The handwriting is a rounded, rather schoolish German Kurrent with later blue-ink corrections (umlauts, the 'y' in Lychnitis). It does not resemble Gauss's mature hand. Together with the subject matter, this suggests a non-mathematical leaf, possibly not by Gauss, bound into or misfiled in the bundle 'HB.Lagrange1816'.
errors: Historical simplification: Philip did not strictly 'cede' (abtreten) Amphipolis to Athens in 359. He withdrew his garrison and renounced his own claim, declaring the city free, to placate Athens.

Chronology compressed: Philip initially ruled as regent/guardian for his nephew Amyntas IV. His acclamation as king is usually dated to c. 357/356 BC, after the 358 victory over Bardylis. The note's sequence is broadly consistent with older textbook accounts.
The Thracian king who backed Pausanias (Berisades or Kotys, depending on the source) is unnamed here. This is not an error, just imprecise.
No mathematical errors are possible; the page has no mathematical content.
